name: NAIC on Artificial Intelligence in Insurance: Topic Overview, Working Group and Health Data Call
title: NAIC on Artificial Intelligence in Insurance: Topic Overview, Working Group and Health Data Call
answer: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners publishes a topic overview of AI in insurance, the mandate of its Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group, and the 2024 Health AI/ML Survey data call. Its most useful content for the industry is the survey evidence: across four lines of business, most responding insurers already use, plan to use or plan to explore AI and machine learning models.

sections.body: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners, the US state insurance regulators' organisation, publishes these pages on content.naic.org. Three are relevant. One is an insurance topic overview explaining what artificial intelligence is and how it is used and regulated in insurance. One is the committee page for the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group, describing its mandate and recent activities. One is the data call page for the Health AI/ML Survey, dated November 11, 2024, when the informational letter and company survey links were issued.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The overview defines AI as technology letting computer systems perform tasks that usually require human intelligence, including analysing data, images, video and sound, summarising information and generating content. Insurers use it in underwriting, pricing, customer service, claims handling, marketing and fraud detection. Chatbots answer common questions and assist with simple transactions at any time of day. Claims processing uses AI to estimate repair costs or assess damage from photos and historical data. AI may move insurers from detect and repair toward predict and prevent, identifying risks earlier so customers avoid losses. Large language models such as CoPilot, ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can answer questions, summarise documents and assist with writing but may generate information that sounds accurate yet is incorrect. AI is more likely to support than replace actuaries, underwriters, claims professionals, agents and customer service representatives. Insurers remain responsible for complying with insurance laws, regulations, standards and consumer protection rules, including fairness, accuracy and avoiding unfair discrimination, and regulators may require companies to explain how tools are used in underwriting, pricing, marketing or claims decisions. The Working Group researches big data and AI in insurance, monitors state, federal and international activity, supports adoption of the Model Bulletin on the Use of AI Systems by Insurers, and coordinates evaluation tools and regulator training. Recent meetings covered the AI Risk Evaluation Supplement, AI governance trends, the AI Systems Evaluation Tool Pilot and Exhibits B to D of that tool.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The NAIC formed the Innovation Cybersecurity and Technology (H) Committee in 2021 and established the Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (H) Working Group in 2019. Regulatory principles on AI were adopted by the full NAIC membership at the 2020 Summer National Meeting. Survey reports for private passenger auto, homeowners, life and health insurance were issued in December 2022, August 2023, December 2023 and May 2025. Of 193 auto insurers responding, 88% reported they use, plan to use or plan to explore AI/ML models; of 194 home insurers, 70%; of 161 life companies, 58%; of 93 health insurers, 92%. The Health AI/ML Survey runs under the examination authorities of 16 states: Colorado, Connecticut, Illinois, Iowa, Louisiana, Maryland, Minnesota, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Vermont, Virginia, West Virginia and Wisconsin. Companies writing health business in one of those states with more than $250 million of earned health insurance premium in 2023, or a significant market share in one of them, must complete it.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: This is the supervisory frame for AI in US insurance, written by the regulators themselves rather than by vendors or consultants. A reader following AI in the industry can use it to see which uses regulators recognise, from chatbots and claims estimation to predict and prevent, and to understand that responsibility for compliance stays with the insurer. The survey results give a rare line of business breakdown of adoption intent, and the Working Group page shows where supervision is heading through the Model Bulletin, the AI Systems Evaluation Tool and its pilot.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Insurance

sections.body: The pages are explanatory and procedural rather than analytical. The overview describes uses and regulatory expectations without evaluating outcomes or naming individual insurers. The survey figures report whether companies use, plan to use or plan to explore AI and machine learning, which combines current adoption with future intent and does not measure deployment depth or results. The Health AI/ML Survey page sets out scope and obligations but not findings. The committee page reports activities and documents under discussion, some still in draft or pilot form, so it is a snapshot of work in progress rather than settled guidance.
